title: The Sharpe Pint

opening_mood.text: Morning. Grab a flat white and pull up a chair. Today we are unpacking Elon Musk's latest $60bn shopping spree using SpaceX's shiny new public paper, a geopolitical peace deal that has sent oil sliding, and why your boss is probably a 'resulting' addict who cannot tell luck from genius. We also have a proper look at the 'shadow default' rate quietly compounding in private credit, a clever way to train trading models without getting your teeth kicked in by transaction costs, and a cold bucket of water for anyone trying to build an LLM-driven trading strategy. Let's get into it.

content.text: Grab your coffee. Today we are unpacking a record-shattering AI acquisition from a newly public rocket company, a massive geopolitical shift that is sending oil prices off a cliff, a high-stakes game of chicken between the bond market and the new Fed Chair, a classic private equity carve-out of a high-street pizza giant, and a bold, capital-heavy gamble in the autonomous vehicle space. Here is what you need to know to look smart in the City today.
1. SpaceX Launches into the AI Coding Wars with $60bn Cursor Acquisition

Just days after its blockbuster Nasdaq IPO—which officially crowned Elon Musk as the world's first trillionaire—SpaceX has pulled off the largest acquisition of a venture-backed startup in history. The rocket-and-satellite giant has agreed to acquire Anysphere, the parent company behind the wildly popular AI coding assistant Cursor, in an all-stock deal valued at a staggering $60 billion. The news sent SpaceX shares climbing, briefly pushing its valuation past Amazon to make it the world's fifth most valuable listed company.

Why does a rocket company need an AI coding agent? It all comes down to xAI, Musk's AI division which was folded into SpaceX earlier this year. Grok has been lagging behind OpenAI and Anthropic, and a recent mass exodus of all 11 of xAI's co-founders left the division in desperate need of a rebuild. By acquiring Cursor—which boasts over 1 million developers and a $2 billion annual revenue run rate—SpaceX is trying to buy its way to the top of the 'vibe coding' revolution.

The City angle: This is a masterclass in using highly valued public paper as a super-currency. Because SpaceX's post-IPO stock has surged by roughly 50% since floating, it can fund a massive $60bn acquisition with minimal dilution. It is a classic tech-bubble playbook: print expensive equity, buy real cash-flowing software assets.

What to say at work: Musk is using SpaceX's newly minted public equity as a weapon. Buying Cursor for $60bn in stock is a massive bet that coding is the ultimate wedge for enterprise AI, but it also shows how desperate they are to fix xAI after the co-founders walked out.
2. Oil Plunges Below $80 as US and Iran Prepare to Sign Peace Deal

The geopolitical premium on crude is deflating fast. The US and Iran have agreed to an interim memorandum of understanding (MoU) to end nearly four months of war, with a formal signing ceremony scheduled for Friday at Switzerland's Burgenstock resort. The deal includes a 60-day ceasefire, the immediate lifting of the US naval blockade, and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Tankers have already started moving, with Iranian crude exports resuming for the first time in two months.

Brent crude plummeted over 5% to trade below $80 a barrel, bringing massive relief to global energy markets. The draft agreement, leaked via Bloomberg, promises Iran sanctions relief and phased access to $300 billion in frozen funds in exchange for stopping hostilities. However, the deal conspicuously avoids thorny issues like Iran's enriched uranium stockpile or its ballistic missile programme.

The City angle: For macro traders and asset managers, this is a major supply-side shock normalisation. Lower energy prices will help cool headline inflation, which has been a persistent thorn in the side of central banks. But because the deal leaves Iran's nuclear ambitions completely unaddressed, the geopolitical risk has not disappeared—it has just been deferred.

What to say at work: The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is a massive relief for global supply chains, but the fact that the MoU completely ignores Iran's nuclear enrichment means this is a highly fragile geopolitical plaster, not a cure.
3. The Bond Market Calls Kevin Warsh's Bluff at His First Fed Meeting

Newly confirmed Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is presiding over his first FOMC meeting this week. While the committee is universally expected to hold interest rates steady, the real drama is the growing chasm between Warsh's political mandate and macroeconomic reality. Trump appointed Warsh in the hope of securing rate cuts, but with US inflation ticking up to a three-year high of 4.2% in May, the bond market is calling his bluff.

Instead of pricing in cuts, Wall Street is actually hedging for rate hikes over the next 12 months. Warsh is also expected to launch a quiet revolution in how the Fed communicates. He is a vocal opponent of forward guidance and the 'dot plot', preferring 'strategic ambiguity' to prevent markets from front-running every central bank utterance.

The City angle: For fixed income desks and quants, the death of forward guidance means volatility is back on the menu. If Warsh successfully kills the dot plot and reduces the frequency of press conferences, markets will have to rely on hard data rather than parsing the Fed's adjectives.

What to say at work: Warsh wants to bring back 'strategic ambiguity' and kill the dot plot to stop the market from front-running the Fed. But with inflation at 4.2% and the bond market pricing in hikes, his political pressure to cut rates is colliding head-on with reality.
4. Yum! Brands Slices Up Pizza Hut in $2.7bn Private Equity Carve-Out

Yum! Brands is finally offloading its persistent underperformer, Pizza Hut, selling the chain for an aggregate of $2.7 billion. The deal is split into two: private equity firm LongRange Capital is buying the non-China business (including US operations) for $1.5 billion, while Yum China Holdings is taking full ownership of the mainland China operations for $1.2 billion.

Pizza Hut has long been the weak link in Yum's portfolio, which also includes KFC and Taco Bell. While Yum's global sales rose 5% last year, Pizza Hut's sales fell 2%, battered by fierce delivery competition from Domino's and a broader consumer shift toward healthier options—partially accelerated by the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.

The City angle: This is a classic portfolio optimisation play. By carving out Pizza Hut, Yum! Brands becomes a more focused, higher-margin business. Shareholders are already cheering, especially with the board approving a fresh $4 billion share buyback authorization alongside the sale. For LongRange Capital, taking the brand private allows them to execute a multi-year turnaround away from the quarterly scrutiny of public markets.

What to say at work: Yum offloading Pizza Hut for $2.7bn is a textbook portfolio clean-up. It lets them focus on KFC and Taco Bell, while giving private equity a classic turnaround play. Plus, the $4bn buyback authorization is a nice sweetener for Yum shareholders.
5. Mobileye Gambles on Vertical Integration with Own Robotaxi Fleet

Autonomous driving pioneer Mobileye has announced a major strategic pivot: it is moving beyond simply supplying self-driving technology to automakers and launching its own vertically integrated robotaxi business. Set to debut in a major U.S. city in 2027, the initiative will combine its 'Mobileye Drive' autonomous system with its Moovit subsidiary's mobility platform to manage everything from fleet operations to consumer-facing ride-hailing apps.

This is a massive shift in business model. Historically, Mobileye has been a high-margin, asset-light software and chip supplier. Operating a physical fleet of driverless cars puts them in direct, capital-intensive competition with Alphabet's Waymo and Tesla's upcoming network.

The City angle: Equity analysts will be closely scrutinising the capital expenditure implications of this move. While vertical integration offers higher long-term revenue potential per mile, it completely alters Mobileye's risk profile, shifting it from a tech provider to a capital-heavy transport operator.

What to say at work: Mobileye's shift to owning its own robotaxi fleet is a massive gamble. They're moving from a high-margin, asset-light software model to a capital-heavy, operationally complex fleet model just to compete with Waymo and Tesla. It shows how hard it is to win the autonomous race purely as a supplier.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: If you spent Tuesday looking at the Dow and the Nasdaq, you’d be forgiven for thinking they were trading on different planets. While the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average notched its fourth straight winning session to close at a fresh record high of 52,016.57 (up 0.64%), the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite slid 1.15% to 26,376.34, and the S&P 500 slipped 0.57% to 7,511.35. This wasn't a panic; it was a classic, aggressive sector rotation. Investors are taking profits from the high-flying AI chip giants and recycling that cash into industrials, financials, and cyclicals.

The catalyst for this rotation is a massive double-whammy of geopolitical relief and central bank positioning. First, the geopolitical side: a provisional U.S.-Iran peace deal announced over the weekend—with a formal signing scheduled for Friday in Switzerland—has completely defanged the oil market. WTI crude tumbled 4% on Tuesday to finish below $80 a barrel for the first time since March, dragging energy prices down more than 10% this week. For traditional, margin-squeezed businesses, cheaper oil is an immediate shot of adrenaline. For tech, it’s a cue to take some chips off the table ahead of today's main event.
The Warsh Era Begins

That main event is, of course, the Federal Reserve's rate decision today. While the market has priced in a 97% probability of a hold at 3.50%–3.75%, this is the first meeting chaired by Kevin Warsh since he succeeded Jerome Powell. The focus isn't on the rate itself, but on the updated 'dot plot' and Warsh's debut press conference. Bank of America’s latest survey showed that 55% of fund managers expect Warsh to strike a hawkish tone, but BofA’s own analysts suspect he might actually lean dovish relative to a highly conservative committee. The market is bracing for how he frames the balance between a robust labor market and sticky inflation.
The Yen Carry Trade: A 31-Year High That Fizzled

Meanwhile, across the Pacific, the Bank of Japan pulled off a historic move on Tuesday, raising its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 1.0%—its highest level since 1995. You’d think a three-decade high would spark a massive short-squeeze on the Yen, but USD/JPY barely budged, continuing to hover just above the 160 mark. Why? Because the BOJ threw a dovish bone to the market by announcing it would halt further tapering of its Japanese Government Bond (JGB) purchases from April 2027, keeping them steady at ¥2 trillion per month. With the U.S.-Japan rate differential still massive, leveraged funds—who had pushed short-yen bets to a nine-year high of over 115,000 contracts last week—saw no reason to panic-unwind their carry trades just yet.
SpaceX and the AI Bubble Jitters

In individual stock land, the semiconductor heavyweights took a proper beating: Nvidia fell 2.4%, Broadcom dropped 4.4%, and Micron Technology lost 6.2% as investors questioned whether the AI infrastructure trade has run too hot. Yet, Elon Musk’s newly listed SpaceX defied the gravity of the tech sell-off, rising 4.8% for its third consecutive gain since its blockbuster IPO last Friday. SpaceX’s valuation is now comfortably north of $2 trillion, fueled further by its announcement of a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding assistant Cursor. Elsewhere, Yum Brands climbed 1.9% after agreeing to offload its struggling Pizza Hut chain to private equity firm LongRange Capital for $2.7 billion.
The Cross-Asset Read: What's Under the Hood?

Underneath the surface, the cross-asset message is clear: the 'inflation panic' of the last four months is rapidly deflating alongside crude oil. The 2-year Treasury yield ticked down slightly to 4.056%, signaling that fixed-income markets are breathing a sigh of relief. If Warsh can deliver a smooth, non-disruptive press conference today without throwing any hawkish hand grenades, the path of least resistance for equities remains upward—but the leadership is shifting. The era of 'buy mega-cap tech and ignore the rest' is giving way to a broader, healthier market breadth where cheap energy and stable rates give the rest of the economy room to run.

content.text: The Shadow Default: Payment-in-Kind (PIK) Interest

Private credit has been the undisputed darling of the City for the last few years. Yields are juicy, covenants are flexible, and direct lenders have happily eaten the banks' lunch. But as higher interest rates have squeezed corporate balance sheets, a quiet financial engineering trick has been working overtime in the background: Payment-in-Kind (PIK) interest. It is the ultimate corporate credit 'kick the can down the road' mechanism, and understanding it is essential for anyone looking at private markets, leveraged finance, or distressed debt.
What is PIK?

Payment-in-Kind does exactly what it says on the tin. Instead of paying interest to lenders in cash, the borrower pays 'in kind' by issuing more debt. The unpaid interest is capitalised—meaning it is tacked onto the principal balance of the loan. This preserves the borrower's cash in the short term, but it triggers an exponential compounding effect on the debt balance.

Imagine a company with a £100m loan at a 10% PIK interest rate:
- Year 0: Principal is £100m.
- Year 1: Instead of paying £10m cash, the interest is capitalised. New principal is £110m.
- Year 2: The 10% interest is calculated on £110m, which is £11m. New principal is £121m.
- Year 5: Without paying a single penny of cash interest, the debt has ballooned to £161m.
Good PIK vs. Bad PIK
In the credit markets, not all PIK is created equal. Lenders and analysts split PIK into two very different categories:

items: Good PIK (Structured at Origination): This is baked into the loan agreement from day one. It is common for high-growth, cash-consumptive businesses (like SaaS or healthcare) where cash is better spent on R&D or bolt-on acquisitions rather than debt service. Lenders charge a premium for this (e.g., 8% cash vs. 10% PIK) to compensate for the deferred cash flow.

Bad PIK (PIK by Amendment): This is the warning flare. It happens mid-loan when a borrower is drowning in cash interest payments and begs the lender for an amendment to switch from cash-pay to PIK. It is a desperate liquidity preservation tactic.

content.text: According to data from Lincoln International and CAIA, 'bad PIK'—interest deferred mid-loan due to liquidity strain—rose to about 6.4% of the private credit market by late 2025. Many credit analysts treat this as a 'shadow default rate'. While the official headline default rate in private credit sits at a comfortable ~2%, the true level of corporate distress is closer to 6% once you count the companies being kept on life support via PIK amendments.
Why Asset Managers and BDCs are Sweating

For Business Development Companies (BDCs) and private credit funds, PIK interest creates a nasty accounting headache known as the 'phantom income' problem. Under tax rules, PIK interest is recognized as taxable income when it accrues, even though no cash has changed hands. Because BDCs are legally required to distribute 90% of their taxable income to shareholders to maintain their tax-exempt status, they are forced to pay out cash dividends on interest they have not actually collected. If a BDC's portfolio becomes too heavily weighted toward PIK (which Fitch Ratings noted rose to over 8% of BDC income in 2025), it can severely drain their cash liquidity.
The Interview Killer: The Three-Statement Walkthrough

If you are interviewing for private equity, private credit, or leveraged finance, you are highly likely to get asked how PIK interest flows through the financial statements. Here is the exact walkthrough for £10m of PIK interest, assuming a 30% tax rate:

items: Income Statement: Interest expense increases by £10m. This reduces pre-tax income by £10m. Assuming a 30% tax rate, Net Income decreases by £7m.

Cash Flow Statement: Net Income starts down by £7m. However, PIK is a non-cash expense, so we add back the £10m of PIK interest. Cash from Operations increases by £3m (which is the tax shield from the interest expense).

Balance Sheet: Cash (Assets) is up by £3m. On the Liabilities side, Debt increases by £10m because the interest was capitalised. Under Equity, Retained Earnings decreases by £7m (from the Net Income drop). Both sides balance perfectly (Assets up £3m, Liabilities & Equity up £3m).

content.text: The Soundbite for the Pub

"The next time someone tells you private credit is bulletproof because defaults are only 2%, ask them about the shadow default rate. With 'bad PIK' amendments sitting around 6%, lenders aren't avoiding defaults—they're just capitalising them and praying for rate cuts before the debt snowball wipes out the equity."

content.text: The Death of Predict-then-Optimize: Direct Sharpe Ratio Optimization

Most early-career quants make the same rookie mistake when applying machine learning to trading: they treat it like a Kaggle competition. They train an LSTM or an XGBoost model to predict tomorrow's asset return, minimising Mean Squared Error (MSE). Then, they slap a heuristic rule on top—like 'if predicted return is positive, buy; if negative, sell.' In the real world, this 'Predict-then-Optimize' workflow is a recipe for getting your teeth kicked in. Why? Because the model is completely blind to risk, volatility, and transaction costs during training. It treats a highly volatile, highly uncertain 1% predicted return exactly the same as a rock-solid, low-volatility 1% predicted return.

Enter Deep Momentum Networks (DMNs) and Direct Sharpe Ratio Optimization. Instead of predicting returns, we train the neural network to directly output our trading positions (e.g., between -1 and 1). We then use a custom, differentiable loss function that calculates the Sharpe ratio of the resulting strategy over a batch of time steps, and backpropagates the gradients. The network learns trend estimation, risk-scaling, and position sizing all in one go.
How It Works (and Why CTAs Care)

In systematic trend-following (the bread and butter of CTAs like Man AHL, Winton, and Systematica), the classic framework requires handcrafting a trend signal (like a MACD crossover) and then scaling the position size by the asset's ex-ante volatility. A Deep Momentum Network replaces this handcrafted pipeline. The inputs are simple: historical returns over different horizons (1-day, 1-month, 3-month) and standard trend indicators. The network (typically an LSTM) outputs a continuous position target between -1 and 1.

Because we use PyTorch or JAX, we can write the Sharpe ratio as a mathematical function of the network's outputs and the actual asset returns. Since every step in this calculation is differentiable, we can backpropagate through the entire backtest. Even better, we can add a turnover regularisation term to penalise the network for chopping and changing its positions too quickly, forcing it to learn to ignore noise and save on execution costs.
The Code: Sharpe Loss with a Turnover Penalty
Here is how you implement this in PyTorch. Notice how we combine the negative Sharpe ratio (since we want to minimise the loss) with an L1 penalty on position changes to represent transaction costs.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SharpeWithTurnoverLoss(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, penalty_weight=0.01, eps=1e-8):
        super().__init__()
        self.penalty_weight = penalty_weight  # Controls transaction cost sensitivity
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, positions, asset_returns):
        # positions: model outputs for each time step, shape (T,)
        # asset_returns: actual returns for each time step, shape (T,)
        
        # Calculate strategy returns at each step
        strategy_returns = positions * asset_returns
        
        mean_ret = torch.mean(strategy_returns)
        std_ret = torch.std(strategy_returns)
        
        # Negative Sharpe ratio (minimising this maximises Sharpe)
        sharpe = mean_ret / (std_ret + self.eps)
        
        # L1 penalty on position changes (turnover)
        turnover = torch.mean(torch.abs(positions[1:] - positions[:-1]))
        
        # Total loss
        loss = -sharpe + self.penalty_weight * turnover
        return loss
The Academic Backing

This approach was popularised by Bryan Lim, Stefan Zohren, and Stephen Roberts from the Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance in their seminal paper, 'Enhancing Time Series Momentum Strategies Using Deep Neural Networks' (2019). They backtested the model on a portfolio of 88 continuous futures contracts. The Sharpe-optimised LSTM outperformed traditional trend-following benchmarks by more than two times in the absence of transaction costs. More importantly, when they introduced the turnover regularisation term, the model maintained its outperformance even when factoring in transaction costs of up to 2 to 3 basis points.
How to Use This in a Pub or Interview Conversation

items: The Setup: 'Most people try to predict returns and then build a portfolio. But that separates prediction from portfolio construction.'
The Pivot: 'Instead, I like the Deep Momentum Network approach. You let an LSTM directly output position sizes and train it by directly optimising the Sharpe ratio of the resulting strategy.'

The Killer Detail: 'But you can't do it naively. You have to include a turnover regularisation term in the loss function. Otherwise, the network will over-trade and eat itself alive in transaction costs. By adding an L1 penalty on position changes, the network naturally learns to ignore short-term noise and only trade when the trend is strong enough to justify the execution cost.'

content.text: The Catch (Because There's Always a Catch)

items: Overfitting the Denominator: Neural networks are incredibly lazy. If the network finds a way to make the standard deviation of returns (the denominator) extremely close to zero, the Sharpe ratio explodes. It might do this by taking tiny, near-zero positions. You need to add constraints or a minimum volatility floor to prevent the model from cheating.

Lookahead Bias in Batches: When calculating the mean and standard deviation over a batch, you must ensure that the position at time t is strictly a function of information available before time t. The loss is calculated globally, but the information flow must remain strictly causal.

Non-Stationarity: If market regimes shift abruptly, a model trained to optimise a historical Sharpe ratio might get caught heavily leveraged on the wrong side of a trend reversal. Combining this with a Changepoint Detection (CPD) module is often required to tell the LSTM when to cut its positions fast.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: Every second person in the City is currently trying to plug a Large Language Model into a trading strategy, an investment memo, or a research workflow. And, surprise surprise, almost all of their backtests look like absolute magic. But before you hand over your capital to the latest 'AI-driven alpha' fund, you need to read a brilliant new paper: 'Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration' (arXiv:2602.14233), published in February 2026.

Written by a stellar lineup of quantitative finance and AI heavyweights—including Stefan Zohren from the Oxford-Man Institute and Alejandro Lopez-Lira (the academic behind the famous ChatGPT-trading paper)—this paper is a cold, refreshing bucket of water over the financial AI hype. The authors reviewed 164 papers on financial LLMs and discovered that almost all of them commit at least one of five 'sins' that make their spectacular results completely useless for real-world deployment.
The Five Sins of Financial LLM Evaluation

items: Look-Ahead Bias (The Time-Traveler): This is the most common trap. It comes in two flavours. First, 'Parametric Knowledge Leakage'—if you backtest an LLM on 2022 data, but the model's training cutoff was 2024, it already knows which tech stocks blew up and which went to zero. Second, 'External Knowledge Leakage'—using a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system that pulls from a database updated with post-event information.

Survivorship Bias (The Ghost Hunter): Evaluating your model only on companies that are still trading today. If your LLM is picking stocks from the S&P 500's current constituents back in 2018, it's ignoring all the firms that went bust in the meantime. Shockingly, only 1.2% of the 164 papers reviewed even mentioned this.

Narrative Bias (The Bullsh*tter): LLMs are designed to be coherent and persuasive. They will spin a beautiful, highly logical story explaining why a stock is going up, even if the underlying data is pure noise. This creates an 'illusion of understanding' that masks a complete lack of predictive power.

Objective Bias (The Overconfident Guess): Forcing a model to make a call (e.g., Buy/Sell) when the correct answer is 'I don't know'. In finance, knowing when to sit on your hands is half the battle. LLMs are incentivised to hallucinate certainty rather than admit ignorance.

Cost Bias (The Paper Tiger): Ignoring transaction fees, slippage, and the actual cost of running the model. An LLM-based strategy might show a 15% paper return, but if it requires 10,000 API calls a day and trades illiquid mid-caps, the execution costs and OpenAI bill will eat your entire margin.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: The Illusion of Validity: Most academic and vendor claims about 'LLM-driven outperformance' are built on contaminated backtests. When these biases compound, they create a massive gap between paper PnL and live performance.
The 1.2% Problem: The fact that only 1.2% of papers account for survivorship bias shows how low the bar currently is for 'financial AI' research.

The Structural Validity Framework: The authors propose a checklist to clean up financial LLM evaluations, focusing on temporal sanitation (making sure the model is truly blind to the future) and realistic cost modeling.

content.text: Finance-specific biases can inflate performance, contaminate backtests, and make reported results useless for any deployment claim... no single bias is discussed in more than 28 percent of studies.
What to Skim vs. What to Read

Skip the heavy math in the user study section unless you're a hardcore ML researcher. Instead, focus on Section 3, which details the 'Five Sins' with concrete financial examples, and the 'Structural Validity Checklist' in Section 4. It's a perfect blueprint for auditing any vendor pitch or internal AI project.
How it Connects to You & What to Say at the Pub

If you're in asset management, quant, or banking, you're going to see a pitch deck or an internal proposal claiming some LLM can predict market moves with 70% accuracy. Now you have the exact questions to tear it apart. Ask them: 'How did you control for parametric knowledge leakage during the backtest?' or 'What was your abstention rate when the model faced high-uncertainty regimes?' You'll instantly sound like the smartest person in the room—or at least the most delightfully cynical.
Our Take

This paper is a public service. The financial industry has a long history of over-fitting simple linear regressions; giving practitioners a tool as powerful as an LLM without strict guardrails was always going to result in spectacular backtest-fitting. If you're building or buying AI tools for investment decisions, this paper isn't optional reading—it's the minimum standard.

content.text: The "Resulting" Trap: Why Your Boss Confuses Luck with Genius

Picture this: You spend three weeks building a flawless, stress-tested valuation model for an acquisition. You hedge every conceivable risk, negotiate a brilliant price, and pull the trigger. Two weeks later, a freak regulatory change—completely out of left field—tanks the target company's sector. Your boss hauls you into a meeting room and asks how you could have made such a "stupid decision". Meanwhile, the analyst at the desk next to you bought a basket of highly speculative, unhedged tech stocks on a gut feeling, watched them rocket 40% on a random retail squeeze, and is currently being paraded around the office as the next Warren Buffett.

Welcome to the frustrating world of "resulting" (or outcome bias). Coined by poker players and popularized by decision theorist Annie Duke in her book Thinking in Bets, resulting is our hardwired tendency to equate the quality of a decision with the quality of its outcome. In an uncertain world, this is a massive intellectual error. Good decisions can lead to bad outcomes, and absolute madness can occasionally make you rich.
The Classic Experiment

In 1988, psychologists Jonathan Baron and John Hershey ran a study that proved just how deep this bias runs. They gave participants a scenario: a doctor has to decide whether to perform a risky but medically necessary surgery on a patient. The odds of success are known and high.

The researchers split the participants into two groups. Group A was told the surgery succeeded; Group B was told the patient died. Despite having the exact same pre-op data and probability calculations, Group B rated the doctor’s decision-making as reckless and incompetent, while Group A hailed the doctor as a brilliant strategist. We are naturally allergic to uncertainty. Our brains crave a neat, moralistic narrative: if the outcome was bad, someone must have screwed up. If the outcome was good, they must be a visionary.
How to Use This in the City
Once you spot resulting, you see it everywhere—from investment committees to annual performance reviews. Here is how you can use this concept to navigate the office:

items: In Performance Reviews: Don't just show up with a list of your successful trades or projects. If you had a great year, explain why your process worked so you don't look like you just got lucky. More importantly, if a project failed due to bad luck (variance), walk your manager through your ex-ante decision-making process. Show them that based on the information available at the time, the bet was highly asymmetric and mathematically correct.

In Team Meetings: When a project or trade goes wrong, stop the post-mortem from turning into a finger-pointing exercise. Ask the team: "If we went back in time with the exact same information we had on day one, would we make this decision again?" If the answer is yes, you didn't make a bad decision—you just got a bad bounce.

In Interviews: When an interviewer asks, "Tell me about a mistake you made," don't give them a generic "I worked too hard" answer. Instead, tell them about a time you had a flawed process that actually resulted in a good outcome, but you caught the error and fixed the process anyway. It shows a level of risk-management maturity that will make any senior PM or MD immediately want to hire you.

content.text: One Line to Remember
A lucky idiot is still an idiot, and a smart bet that loses is still a smart bet.
